chapters.name: Chapter 1: Three AI workflows for leaders

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Meeting notes to action list
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn rough meeting notes into a clear action list with owners and dates.
This lesson builds toward: Given rough notes from a real meeting with personal details removed, you will use a reusable prompt to turn the notes into decisions, actions with owners and dates, and open questions, checking the list for anything invented or missing.
Meetings end in vague memory more often than in clear actions. AI is good at turning rough notes into structure. Paste your notes (with personal or confidential details removed) and ask for a list of decisions, actions with an owner and a due date, and open questions.
A reusable prompt: "From these meeting notes, list: 1) decisions made, 2) actions as a table with task, owner, due date, 3) open questions. If an owner or date is missing, write MISSING. Do not add anything not in the notes." The last sentence matters: it stops the tool from inventing tasks.
Many meeting apps now offer AI notes or summaries. Before turning them on, check your organization's policy and tell participants, because recording and transcribing people raises consent and privacy questions.
Step by step:
- Remove personal or confidential details from the notes.
- Paste the notes with the reusable prompt.
- Check every action against your memory and the notes.
- Fill in anything marked MISSING.
- Send the list to attendees the same day.
Words to know:
- Action item: a task agreed in a meeting, with an owner and a due date.
- Reusable prompt: a prompt you save and use again for the same kind of task.
Try it now: Take notes from a recent meeting, remove personal details, run the reusable prompt, and check the result. Count anything it got wrong or invented.
You can now turn meeting notes into a checked action list with owners and dates.

check.q: What should a good meeting-notes prompt ask the AI to list?
options: Who talked the most
Decisions, actions with owners and dates, and open questions
A summary of every sentence
Ideas for the next meeting's snacks
check.why: Decisions, owned actions and open questions are what a team needs after a meeting.

check.q: The action list includes a task nobody mentioned in the meeting. What would you do?
options: Keep it, since it is a good idea
Assign it to yourself quietly
Remove it and add "Do not add anything not in the notes" to the prompt
Ask the AI to explain why
check.why: Invented tasks cause confusion; the prompt rule stops the tool from adding them.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: The decision memo: options, risks and a recommendation
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Use AI to draft a decision memo that compares options fairly.
This lesson builds toward: Given a real decision you face, you will draft a decision memo with options, risks and follow-up questions, then write the recommendation yourself, never giving "AI recommended it" as a reason.
Leaders decide under time pressure. AI can help you think wider, not decide for you. Give it the decision, the facts you have, your constraints (budget, time, people) and ask for three options, each with benefits, risks, costs and what you would need to believe for it to be the best choice.
Then push back: "What is the strongest argument against my preferred option?" and "What information am I missing?" These two follow-ups are where AI adds the most value, because they surface blind spots.
You write the recommendation. Check every number, add what only you know (your people, your history, your values) and own the decision. The memo should never say "AI recommended" as a reason.
Step by step:
- Describe the decision, facts and constraints (no private data).
- Ask for three options with benefits, risks and costs.
- Ask for the strongest argument against your favorite.
- Ask what information is missing.
- Check numbers and write the recommendation yourself.
Words to know:
- Decision memo: a short document that sets out a decision, the options and a recommendation.
- Blind spot: something important you have not noticed.
Try it now: Pick a real decision you face (for example, a new schedule, a vendor or an event). Run the decision-memo prompt and both follow-ups, then write a one-paragraph recommendation in your own words.
You can now use AI to widen a decision and write a memo you own.

check.q: What is AI's best role in a decision memo?
options: Making the final decision
Choosing which option the team prefers
Signing the memo
Widening your options and finding blind spots
check.why: AI helps you see more options and risks; the leader decides.

check.q: You have a favorite option. Which follow-up would you send?
options: "What is the strongest argument against my preferred option?"
"Tell me my option is best."
"Write the memo shorter."
"Pick for me."
check.why: Asking for the strongest counterargument tests your choice fairly.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Clear team communication
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Draft and adjust a team message for tone, length and audience.
This lesson builds toward: Given three bullets for a team update, you will draft and adjust a team message for tone, length and audience, reading it aloud before sending.
Many leadership problems are communication problems. AI helps you draft a team update, an announcement or a thank-you quickly, then adjust it: "shorter", "warmer", "for staff who are new", "plain English for second-language readers".
Give it your key points as bullets and your audience, and ask for a draft in your voice. Paste an older message you wrote and say "match this tone" to make it sound like you.
Read it aloud before sending. Cut anything you would not say in person. For sensitive news such as layoffs, policy changes or safety incidents, AI may help you structure it, but HR or legal should review the final words and you should deliver important news in person where you can.
Step by step:
- Write your key points as bullets.
- Name the audience and the tone.
- Ask for a draft; give an older message to match your voice.
- Adjust with one or two follow-ups.
- Read it aloud; get review for sensitive news.
Words to know:
- Tone: how a message feels: warm, formal, urgent, calm.
- Audience: the people who will read the message.
Try it now: Write three bullets for a real team update. Use AI to draft it, ask for one adjustment, read it aloud and send it (or save it to send).
You can now draft and adjust team messages with AI while keeping your own voice.

check.q: How do you make an AI draft sound like you?
options: Ask it to use formal language
Paste an older message you wrote and say "match this tone"
Send it without reading
Use more exclamation marks
check.why: An example of your own writing shows the tool your tone.

check.q: The AI's team update is twice as long as you need. What would you do?
options: Send it anyway
Start a new chat with a new tool
Delete the second half
Ask for one adjustment, such as "cut this to five short sentences", then read it aloud
check.why: One clear follow-up fixes length, and reading aloud catches what you would not say.

chapters.name: Chapter 2: People, tools and team guidelines

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Preparing for people conversations without handing them over
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to prepare for a hard conversation while keeping personal data out.
This lesson builds toward: Before a hard people conversation, you will prepare an opening line and questions with AI using only a general description, with no names or private details, and the conversation and decision kept by you.
Feedback, conflict and performance conversations are where leaders most want help and where AI is most dangerous. Personal details about an employee are confidential; do not paste names, health, discipline records or performance ratings into public AI tools.
You can still prepare. Describe the situation in general terms ("a team member often misses deadlines, is well liked, and recently had a family change") and ask for: an opening line, questions to understand their side, and ways to agree next steps. Ask it to role-play the other person so you can practice.
Never let AI decide on hiring, discipline, pay or firing, and never send AI-written feedback you have not rewritten in your own words. People can tell, and trust is what you lose.
Step by step:
- Describe the situation generally, with no names or private details.
- Ask for an opening, questions and next-step options.
- Practice with a role-play.
- Write your own notes in your own words.
- Keep decisions about people with people.
Words to know:
- Role-play: practicing a conversation with someone (or an AI) playing the other person.
- Confidential: information that must be kept private and shared only with people who need it.
Try it now: Think of a conversation you need to have. Describe it in general terms with no names, ask for an opening line and three questions, then role-play it once.
You can now prepare for hard conversations with AI while protecting people's privacy and your trust.

check.q: What may you put into a public AI tool when preparing for a performance conversation?
options: The employee's name and review history
A general description with no names or private details
Their medical notes, to be sensitive
Their full personnel file
check.why: Only a general description keeps the person's private information out of the tool.

check.q: AI suggests exactly what to say and what decision to make about an employee. What do you do?
options: Use its opening line idea as practice, and make the decision yourself
Read its script word for word
Let the AI send the message
Copy its decision into HR records
check.why: AI can help you prepare, but the conversation and decision stay with you.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Choosing and using AI tools wisely
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Compare AI tools on the questions that matter for your team.
This lesson builds toward: Given an AI tool your team uses or wants, you will compare it on data, access and plan terms using the provider's own pages, ending with a one-line verdict: approve, approve with limits, or not yet.
There are many AI tools: general assistants (ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot, Google Gemini, Claude), assistants inside tools you already use (Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Canva, meeting apps), and agent features that can take actions. Features and prices change often.
Ask five questions before your team adopts one. Data: does it store or train on what we type, and can we turn that off? Access: what can it read or do in our systems? Approval: has our organization or IT approved it? Accuracy: can it show sources? Cost: what does it cost per person, now and at renewal?
Find the answers on the provider's own privacy and pricing pages and in your contract, not in ads. Business and education plans often have different data terms from free personal plans; read them for the plan you would actually use.
Step by step:
- List the tools your team uses or wants.
- Check data: storage and training on your inputs.
- Check access: what it can read or do.
- Check approval, accuracy and cost.
- Use the provider's own pages and your contract.
Words to know:
- Data terms: the rules for how a provider stores and uses what you type.
- Built-in assistant: an AI feature inside a tool you already use, like a word processor.
Try it now: Pick one AI tool your team uses or wants. Answer the five questions using the provider's own pages. Write a one-line verdict: approve, approve with limits, or not yet.
You can now judge an AI tool on data, access, approval, accuracy and cost.

check.q: What does the "access" question about an AI tool ask?
options: How much it costs
How fast it answers
What it can read or do in your systems
Which languages it speaks
check.why: Access tells you what the tool could see or change if something goes wrong.

check.q: Your team uses a free personal plan and you want to know if it trains on your data. Where do you look?
options: A news article from last year
The provider's own privacy terms for that plan
A colleague's guess
The AI's own answer in a chat
check.why: Free and business plans can have different data terms, and the provider's pages are the source.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Writing a one-page team AI use guide
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Write a short AI use guide your team can follow.
This lesson builds toward: For your team, you will write a one-page AI use guide and save your tested prompts in one place, covering approved tools, what never goes in, what to check, disclosure and who to ask.
A one-page guide beats a long policy nobody reads. It answers five questions: Which tools may we use? What never goes in? What must a person check before it goes out? When do we say AI helped? Who do we ask?
Write it in plain words with examples from your team's work: "Never paste customer names, addresses or payment details." "A person checks every fact, number and quote." "Tell the customer if they are chatting with an AI." If your organization has a formal policy, your guide must fit inside it; check with HR, IT or legal.
Use AI to draft it from your notes, then edit hard. Share it, ask the team what is unclear, and review it every few months, because tools and risks keep changing.
Step by step:
- Answer the five questions in bullet notes.
- Use AI to draft one page from your notes.
- Add real examples from your team's work.
- Check it fits any organization policy.
- Share it, ask what is unclear, set a review date.
Words to know:
- AI use guide: a short set of rules for how a team uses AI tools.
- Disclosure: telling people that AI helped make something or that they are talking to AI.
Try it now: Final task: save your three tested prompts (meeting actions, decision memo, team update) in one document, and add your one-page team AI use guide with tools, never-put-in, must-check, disclosure and who to ask. Share it with one colleague for feedback.
You can now lead your team's day-to-day AI use with a tested toolkit and a clear one-page guide.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Meeting actions prompt No saved prompt, or it was not tested on real notes. A saved prompt that turns notes into actions with owners and dates, used once with private details removed. The prompt marks missing owners and forbids invented tasks. Decision memo prompt No saved prompt, or the AI made the recommendation. A saved prompt for options and risks, used once, with the recommendation written by the leader. Includes follow-ups that test the preferred option. Team update prompt No saved prompt, or the message was not checked. A saved prompt for team updates, used once and adjusted for tone or length. Includes a sample of the leader's own writing to match tone. One-page AI guide Missing approved tools, what never goes in, what must be checked or who to ask. One page covering approved tools, what never goes in, what a person must check and who to ask. Also covers disclosure and was shared with a colleague for feedback. Private details kept out A prompt or example contains names or private details. No personal or confidential details in any saved prompt or example. Prompts use placeholders such as [team member] so they are safe to reuse. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: What does disclosure mean in a team AI guide?
options: Sharing your passwords with IT
Listing every AI tool ever made
Publishing your prompts online
Telling people when AI helped or when they are talking to AI
check.why: Disclosure keeps people informed about where AI was used.

check.q: Your organization has a formal AI policy. How should your one-page team guide relate to it?
options: Fit inside it and point to it
Replace it with simpler rules
Ignore it, since teams are different
Copy it word for word, all of it
check.why: A team guide adds practical detail but must stay within the organization's policy.
